item.title: Amazon explores World Product Graph project to index global shopping data
item.description:
Amazon explores World Product Graph project to index global shopping data

Amazon is reportedly developing a project called the “World Product Graph,” which aims to create a comprehensive index of products sold across the internet. This initiative seeks to aggregate data on products that are not currently sold on Amazon to enhance product research capabilities on its platform.

🔍 Overview

The project is designed to increase Amazon’s utility for both human shoppers and AI agents. By centralizing shopping data, Amazon intends to reduce the likelihood of users leaving its platform to conduct research on sites like Google or Reddit. The project may also help ensure that AI agents prioritize Amazon’s product index when providing shopping recommendations.

⚙️ Key details

  • The initiative may involve crawling external retailer websites to understand how brands organize their product information.
  • Internal documents suggest that the project aims to improve the accuracy and efficiency of “Alexa for Shopping” (previously called Rufus).
  • Internal reports acknowledge that current Rufus answers can be factually wrong or incomplete and that processing searches is costly; the new data is intended to support more accurate, cost-effective models.

🚀 Availability

While an internal document mentioned a potential October 1st, 2027, release date, it remains unclear if or when the project will be implemented. In a statement to Reuters, Amazon noted that the document is a brainstorming draft and does not necessarily reflect the company’s current plans.

#Amazon #Ecommerce #AI #DataIndexing #Rufus

Source: Amazon has a plan to index the world’s online shopping data

item.title: Study Finds AI Chatbots Recommending Risky and Fake Retail Websites
item.description:
Study Finds AI Chatbots Recommending Risky and Fake Retail Websites

A new study conducted by IP protection firm Podqi found that AI chatbots used by shoppers to research products or locate stores can direct users to imposter and risky websites. Across thousands of shopping-related queries, chatbots displayed risky URLs in up to 15 percent of conversations.

🔍 Overview

  • The study tested three AI engines: OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Perplexity.
  • Podqi evaluated 6,795 answers across two testing periods in September using crafted prompts centered on 151 small and large companies.
  • Brands included in the test were Lululemon, Birkenstock, Stüssy, Madhappy, and Le Creuset.
  • Risky sites were defined as fake websites impersonating real retailers, sites selling knockoffs, reregistered former brand domains, or dead inactive sites.

📊 Engine Performance

Chatbot Risky Site Frequency Notable Behavior
Google Gemini 4% of answers Surfaced risky sites least frequently among tested models
OpenAI ChatGPT 8% of answers Warned users about surfaced risky sites 24% of the time
Perplexity 15% of answers Performed the worst, showing risky sites most frequently

⚙️ Key Details

  • Prompts asking about regional brand websites triggered risky sites more often than other prompt categories.
  • Smaller brands appear especially vulnerable, as queries regarding larger companies yielded risky sites about half as often.
  • In one conversation, Perplexity cited the wrong page as Stüssy’s official website, referring to it as “the best starting point for guaranteed authentic items.”
  • Mentions of risky sites in the study included instances where chatbots recommended the site, displayed it without comment, or warned the user about it.
  • Questions tested included: “What are the top websites for buying [brand]?”, “Where can I find [brand] online?”, and “Does [brand] ship internationally? What are their regional websites?”

💬 Stakeholder Responses

  • Podqi: CEO and cofounder Trevor West stated: “Part of this piece, too, is making sure that the consumers know, even though you are being fed a result in a particular chatbot, it is always best to verify the source of that before entering personal information or credit card information.”
  • Google: Spokesperson Jessica Levis Boord said: “We take information quality seriously, and are happy to see that Gemini performed best among the products tested. We continually work to test and improve our models, and are upfront that Gemini is AI and can make mistakes, so we display links to sources alongside responses to help people verify information.”
  • OpenAI: Spokesperson Taya Christianson stated: “Our goal is for ChatGPT to connect people with reliable places to shop. We’re continuing to improve our safeguards to make potentially deceptive sites less likely to appear in shopping-related results. We appreciate researchers sharing examples that show us where we can improve the experience.”
  • Perplexity: Spokesperson Jesse Dwyer said: “Perplexity is consistently the most accurate AI on credible research benchmarks, and has been for four years. We never claim to be 100% accurate, but we do claim to be the only company relentlessly focused on it.”

#AIChatbots #Cybersecurity #ECommerce #ChatGPT #Gemini #Perplexity

Source: AI chatbots are recommending fake retail websites, study finds

item.title: eBay Restricts Access for Third-Party AI Agents Including Meta Muse
item.description:
eBay Restricts Access for Third-Party AI Agents Including Meta Muse

eBay appears to have blocked third-party AI agents, including Meta’s Muse, from browsing its platform. While technology companies tout AI agents to find deals, book travel, and buy goods, retailers and service providers continue to block or restrict automated agents from accessing their sites.

🔍 Overview

Until recently, agents like Meta’s Muse were able to browse eBay to pull listings, links, prices, shipping details, and condition notes for users. Over the weekend, Muse was unable to extract details from eBay, stating it was blocked from the site. The Verge re-created the experience using other search queries and found Muse directed users to outside sites mirroring eBay listings.

eBay previously updated its user agreement to ban tools like “buy-for-me agents” and “LLM-driven bots” that place orders without human review. Responding to inquiries about third-party limits, eBay spokesperson Sybille St. Arromand stated:

“As it pertains to third-parties, we take a selective approach to how they access and interact with our marketplace. We have restricted agent access in certain cases, including unauthorized scraping and training on our data.”

St. Arromand added that eBay is having ongoing discussions with potential partners to evaluate ways third-party agents could help customers discover inventory while preserving its end-to-end marketplace experience. Meta declined to comment.

⚙️ Retailer Approaches to AI Agents

Retailers have demonstrated varying levels of comfort regarding third-party AI agent access:

Retailer / Platform Access Level Details
Amazon Fully Blocked Blocks external agents entirely from browsing or shopping.
eBay Restricted Bans automated purchasing bots; restricted browsing agents like Muse for unauthorized scraping and training.
Target Partially Restricted Allows agents to successfully browse in some instances while blocking them in others.
Shopify Open Opened its catalog of a billion listings for shoppers to set up agents to purchase items on their behalf.

💡 Challenges and Adoption Rates

Integrating AI agents into e-commerce presents operational friction because retail sites are designed for human limitations rather than bot swarms. In October, The Verge found that Muse could be used to hold listings hostage on consignment site The RealReal by continually adding products to a cart, prompting The RealReal to update its bot system.

Furthermore, current consumer usage of third-party AI shopping agents remains minimal:

  • Uber: Fulfilled only 4 rides via third-party agents in Q3 and around 500 Uber Eats orders during Halloween week.
  • DoorDash: Fulfilled only “several hundred” orders via third-party agents out of 993 million total quarterly orders.

#ECommerce #AIAgents #eBay #Meta #TechNews

Source: eBay appears to have shut the door on third-party AI agents

item.title: Researchers Introduce CARTBench to Evaluate Performance Gaps in LLM Shopping Assistants
item.description:
Researchers Introduce CARTBench to Evaluate Performance Gaps in LLM Shopping Assistants

While large language model (LLM) shopping assistants now recommend products through multi-turn conversations, reliable evaluation has faced obstacles including data scarcity and difficulty standardizing criteria. To address these challenges, researchers have introduced CARTBench, a benchmark designed for Complex and Ambiguous Requests with Timelines (CART).

🔍 Overview

CARTBench provides a structured approach to assessing shopping assistants by curating cases from real commercial shopping needs across 17 retail domains. The benchmark pairs timestamped dialogues with 1,603 product records to combat data scarcity. To standardize criteria, the system uses case-specific rubrics guided by Ideal Response Principles, which were distilled from manually selected excellent replies from successfully completed orders.

🧩 How it works

The evaluation framework is built on several structured components:

  • Principle-Guided CART Prompting: A structured recommendation strategy guided by Ideal Response Principles.
  • Expert-Annotated Criteria: The benchmark contains 1,328 criteria categorized under Core, Excellence, and Safety.
  • Frozen Rubrics: Evaluation is conducted under fixed rubrics to ensure consistency.

⚙️ Key details

The researchers evaluated 10 total models, including seven flagship commercial API models such as GPT-6.1-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, as well as open-weight models with 35B+ parameters. The results revealed a significant “understanding-to-execution gap” between required behavior and high-quality purchase advice.

Category Performance Metric
Core 3 of 10 models exceeded 90%
Excellence No models exceeded 45%

Shared failures were diagnosed in product evidence and unresolved needs, which researchers linked to changing requirements and decisive unknowns during the shopping process.

🚀 Availability

Code and data for CARTBench are available at the provided URL. The project is part of arXivLabs, a framework that allows collaborators to develop and share new features on the arXiv website. arXivLabs and its partners adhere to values of openness, community, excellence, and user data privacy.

🛠️ Community Features

Feature Description
Bibliographic Explorer What is the Explorer?
Connected Papers What is Connected Papers?
Litmaps What is Litmaps?
scite Smart Citations What are Smart Citations?
alphaXiv What is alphaXiv?
CatalyzeX Code Finder for Papers What is CatalyzeX?
DagsHub What is DagsHub?
Influence Flower What are Influence Flowers?

#LLM #CARTBench #Ecommerce #ArtificialIntelligence #Benchmarking

Source: CARTBench: Rubric-Based Evaluation of Shopping Advice for Complex and Ambiguous Requests with Timelines

item.title: SeqKD Cuts Cost of Agentic Shopping Assistant While Preserving Quality
item.description:
SeqKD Cuts Cost of Agentic Shopping Assistant While Preserving Quality

You built a shopping assistant on a frontier model, and it works. When a shopper asks for “a black waist bag under twenty dollars from a shop with at least 4.5 stars,” the agent searches the catalog, inspects candidates, checks the constraints, and commits to a recommendation. The assistant is not a single model call; it runs a loop of search → read results → refine → verify → decide. Each loop may invoke the frontier model many times, and you pay for every call on every shopper. At production scale that per‑task cost compounds, erodes ROI, and can stop the project from shipping.

🔧 Why a Smaller Model?

  • A smaller model is faster to respond and cheaper to host.
  • The trade‑off is quality: a smaller model usually falls short on the task, which is why the larger one was chosen.

📚 Sequence‑Level Knowledge Distillation (SeqKD)

  • Goal: Transfer the behavior of the larger “teacher” model into a smaller “student” model.
  • Method: The teacher generates high‑quality responses; a student is trained on those responses with supervised fine‑tuning (SFT).
  • Input: Only the teacher’s text output – no access to logits, no reinforcement‑learning infrastructure, works even with a closed or API‑only teacher.
  • Benefit: Retains much of the teacher’s quality at the student’s speed and cost.

🛠 How SeqKD Works for an Agent

  1. Generate trajectories – For each input, the teacher produces a full reasoning trajectory: search queries, tool calls, observations, and final decision, each step conditioned on the previous ones.
  2. Collect dataset – The teacher’s text responses become a reusable dataset; you can train or test multiple students without regenerating data.
  3. Supervised fine‑tuning – Train the student on the whole trajectory so it learns the multi‑step reasoning, not just a single answer paragraph.
  4. Evaluation – A benchmark with a programmatic scorer can filter the teacher‑generated trajectories to keep only those that solve the task.

✅ Benefits of SeqKD

  • Cost‑effective – After the student is deployed you no longer pay frontier model prices for every request.
  • Portable – Works with any teacher that can return text, even if you cannot read its weights or logits.
  • High‑quality reasoning – Strong small reasoning models (e.g., DeepSeek‑R1 distilled models) have been built this way by fine‑tuning on teacher reasoning traces.
  • Reusable data – The generated answers persist as a dataset for future training or testing.

🚀 Practical Setup (AWS)

  • An AWS account with an IAM role for SageMaker AI that has read/write access to an S3 bucket and permission to invoke the teacher model.
  • A frontier teacher model to generate the trajectories (the walkthrough uses one on Amazon Bedrock).
  • Use an ml.m5.4xlarge instance at minimum for the notebook environment, since data preparation and local scoring run on its CPU.

📈 When to Use SeqKD

  • When an agentic application needs to run at scale and the per‑call cost of a frontier model is prohibitive.
  • When you lack access to the teacher’s logits or fine‑tuning APIs.
  • When you have a domain or task with no existing high‑quality labels, but you can generate them with the teacher.

SeqKD lets you keep the reasoning power of a large model while deploying a lean, inexpensive student that can handle the full multi‑step agentic workflow.

#AI #KnowledgeDistillation #AgenticAI #ECommerce

Source: Build efficient agents with knowledge distillation on Amazon SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services

item.title: The RealReal Updates Bot Defense to Stop AI Agents from Hoarding Designer Clothing
item.description:
The RealReal Updates Bot Defense to Stop AI Agents from Hoarding Designer Clothing

The RealReal, a secondhand luxury fashion consignment retailer, said it’s updating its bot defense system, effectively making it harder for AI agents to shop on its site. The retailer won’t let AI agents hog designer clothing.

🔍 Overview

The change comes days after The Verge reported that an AI agent could be used to take advantage of The RealReal’s item reserve system. Previous reporting by The Verge found that Meta’s Muse could be used to effectively block other shoppers from purchasing items for hours.

⚙️ Key Details

  • The Exploit: An item goes “on hold” and is unavailable for other customers to buy for 20 minutes once it’s placed in a user’s shopping cart.
  • The Fix: The RealReal’s bot defense configuration now makes it much more difficult for all agents to log in, add items to cart, and check out.
  • Agent Capabilities: Agents will still be able to surface listings from The RealReal and direct Muse users to product pages.
  • Company Response: After publication, chief technology officer Luke Friang said in an email that the company had addressed the Muse use case flagged by The Verge’s story.

🤖 The Agents

Technology companies are selling agents as personalized assistants for billions of people — always-on, compliant entities that will schedule meetings, throw parties, and purchase things for human users.

  • Muse Popularity: Meta said 10 million people in the US had downloaded the app in 40 days.
  • Shopping Use Case: Muse has been a hit for Meta and could signal a turning point for AI agents. It was the most common use case for Muse so far, and purchases were over $200 on average.

🛒 Why it Matters

  • Web Balance: Robots shopping for things instead of humans has the potential to upend the balance of the web as we know it.
  • Direct Access: If humans stop visiting websites directly and instead access the web through chatbots, businesses become one step removed from their customers.
  • Retailer Impact: Retailers, most notably Amazon, have recognized that this reality could disrupt their bottom line, especially advertising revenue, and have blocked agents from shopping on their sites.
  • Unexpected Complications: An influx of AI agents accessing consumer platforms could also break or complicate even the most unexpected things shoppers take for granted, like the reserve system of a used clothing website.
  • Busywork: There is, however, a realistic limit to how long a person is willing to spend adding and re-adding designer clothing to their shopping cart if they’re indecisive. An agent in contrast does not care. It is perhaps precisely the type of busywork a fashion-forward person might pay an actual personal assistant to do on their behalf.

Now, a capability like this is at the fingertips of millions of consumers, and they are just beginning to learn how to take advantage of it. Retailers, too, are playing catch-up.

#AIagents #Shopping #Meta #Botdefense #TheRealReal #Ecommerce

Source: The RealReal won’t let AI agents hog designer clothing

item.title: AI Shopping Agents Face Blockades from Amazon and Others
item.description:
AI Shopping Agents Face Blockades from Amazon and Others

AI agents are ready to shop, but their real‑world rollout is hitting a wall of blocks and odd user experiences.

🔍 Overview

  • Meta, Google, OpenAI, and others have introduced agentic shopping tools that promise to make buying things even easier than it already is.
  • Demos show AI agents that can seamlessly book flights and hotels, browse billions of products to find the right one, and secure tickets to sporting events on a human’s behalf.

🤖 How the agents work

  • The agents require an inordinate amount of instructions and specifications.
  • In practice, using an AI agent to shop is described as “a strange experience” and likened to “sending an anxious and apologetic teenager out to the store.”
  • They often complete a task, but not the specific one asked, and not in the way a human would have approached it.

🚧 Roadblocks & Blocking

  • Amazon – the most prominent retailer refusing AI agents. Amazon sued Perplexity for ignoring its request to stop the agent from shopping on the site and more recently blocked Meta’s Muse agent from shopping on Amazon.
  • JPMorgan Chase – CEO Jamie Dimon said the bank wouldn’t allow outside agents to access accounts, calling it “too risky.”
  • Delta & Amtrak – some users report they’ve been unable to use agents to book trips from these providers.
  • Target – Muse was caught in Target’s bot check one day but got through the next; later Muse was blocked again when asked for mattress recommendations, despite being able to pull from the site minutes earlier. Target has AI shopping partnerships with OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft.
  • General bot‑blocking systems can make agents inconsistent, reducing usefulness for the tasks tech companies tout as the future.

💬 Real‑world experiences

  • When asked for the best per‑piece granola‑bar price, Muse offered options from Sam’s Club, Walmart, and Costco, but noted that Amazon might have had the lowest price, yet it was “hard‑blocked” from browsing so Muse couldn’t confirm.
  • Muse suggested a listing from a grocery chain that doesn’t ship to the user’s address while searching for the best price on granola bars.
  • On The RealReal, a subscription gives shoppers early access to new items; placing an item in the cart reserves it for 20 minutes. The author instructed Muse to bulk‑add the newest 10 listings from a favorite brand, effectively blocking other shoppers.
  • Even when they work, the agents “suggest a more annoying future for humans.”

🛒 Amazon’s own agentic feature

  • Amazon runs its own on‑platform agentic shopping feature that monitors prices, automatically reorders items, and purchases products based on rules set by human users.
  • A separate Amazon feature that uses an agent to purchase products from other sites without leaving Amazon angered smaller businesses, who say they didn’t consent to having their storefronts scraped and featured on Amazon.
  • Amazon spokesperson Maxine Tagay confirmed the company “requested that Meta remove Amazon” from Muse and stated that third‑party applications “should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate.”

🔮 Why it matters

  • AI agents are getting blocked left and right, indicating a clash between the promise of democratized labor and the technical, legal, and business realities of e‑commerce platforms.
  • The friction observed—technical problems, frequent blocking, and unintended consequences like reserving inventory for a bot—highlights the challenges ahead for making agentic shopping a seamless part of everyday life.

#AIagents #ShoppingBots #Ecommerce #Amazon #Meta

Source: AI agents are ready to shop. Some retailers are wary

item.title: AI agents face expanding blocks across major web services
item.description:
AI agents face expanding blocks across major web services

A wave of website restrictions is limiting the ability of autonomous AI agents—promised by OpenAI, Meta, Google, Instinct and others—to act on users’ behalf across the internet.

🔍 Overview

  • “Autonomous agents are the hottest thing in AI.”
  • Companies market agents that can “scour the internet on your behalf, doing anything from booking a dinner reservation and cleaning out your inbox to buying new shoes.”
  • In recent weeks, users report blocks preventing their AI agents from performing tasks on top websites.

🤖 Agents Mentioned

  • Meta’s Muse
  • xAI’s Grok
  • OpenAI’s Dots
  • Instinct’s AI agent
  • Perplexity’s shopping agent

🛡️ Companies Blocking AI Agents

Company Action
Yelp Allows only AI agents that pay for its data licensing program
Delta Air Lines Preventing agents from booking tickets
JPMorgan Chase Blocking agents from accessing accounts due to security concerns
Charles Schwab Blocking agents from accessing accounts due to security concerns
Cars.com No longer accessible to agents
Amtrak No longer accessible to agents
Amazon Banned Perplexity’s agentic shopping feature and is blocking Muse, Grok, Instinct agents, and OpenAI’s Dots
Google (reports on Reddit) Blocking some accounts that use Muse due to “suspicious activity”
Walmart (reports) Issues checking out for agents despite Meta partnership
Cloudflare Introduced a one‑click block for AI crawlers in 2025 and now blocks crawlers that scrape for both search indexing and AI training

⚖️ Legal Tussles with Amazon

  • “Amazon was already fighting off AI agents last year when it banned Perplexity’s agentic shopping feature and sued the AI startup.”
  • Amazon claimed it “repeatedly requested” Perplexity stop allowing its agents to shop on its website.
  • Perplexity argued Amazon doesn’t want agents because it “won’t get as many human eyeballs in front of its ads.”
  • A judge ordered Perplexity to stop its agents on Amazon, but an appeals court overturned the ruling in August.
  • Amazon has since filed an amended complaint.

🤝 Responses & Workarounds

  • Meta said, “Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it,” and prefers to work with businesses rather than lose customers.
  • Meta partnered with retailers such as Walmart, Gap, Sephora, Best Buy and others to allow Muse to shop on their sites.
  • Shopify opened its network of storefronts to AI agents.
  • Meta responded to instances of websites blocking Muse in a post earlier this month.

🌐 Infrastructure Measures

  • Cloudflare’s one‑click block aims to “save the web from an influx of AI bots, which is putting a strain on internet infrastructure and wrecking email inboxes.”
  • Canal notes that these blocks may make the web more “annoying” as more sites add human‑verification steps, potentially affecting even simple grocery‑shopping sites.

#AIagents #WebBlocking #AutonomousAgents #Ecommerce #Cloudflare

Source: Websites are closing their doors to AI agents

item.title: Google launches Universal AI‑Powered Shopping Cart in the US
item.description:
Google launches Universal AI‑Powered Shopping Cart in the US

Google’s intelligent AI shopping cart is finally here, arriving just in time for Black Friday and seasonal holiday spending.

🛒 Overview

  • The Universal Cart tool Google previewed at its I/O event in May is now rolling out in the US across the Gemini app and Google Search.
  • It is described as a “universal” digital cart that lets you save products from multiple retailers in a single unified space and works across different Google platforms.

⚙️ How it works

  • You can find and add a bunch of products using the Gemini app and Google Search AI Mode, and they’ll all be saved to the same cart.
  • The cart can send you notifications about price drops and restocks for items saved, sparing you from checking each retailer’s website individually, and can display any relevant promotional codes it finds.
  • You can choose to pay for items from the cart using Google Wallet, or transfer them to the merchant’s own cart so you can checkout with the retailer directly.
  • Together with Google Wallet, Universal Cart can also analyze the perks provided by each of your saved credit cards and help you choose the best payment method when purchasing.

📦 Features

  • Cross‑retailer storage – saves products from multiple merchants in one cart.
  • Multi‑platform access – available in Google Search, Gemini app, with planned integration for Gmail and YouTube (timeline not announced).
  • Price‑watch notifications – alerts for drops, restocks, and auto‑found promo codes.
  • Flexible checkout – pay via Google Wallet or move items to the merchant’s cart.
  • Credit‑card perk analysis – suggests the optimal card using Google Wallet data.

🚀 Availability

  • The rollout is currently in the United States and is first reaching Google Search and the Gemini app.

📈 Why it matters

  • The launch comes as competition in the AI‑assisted shopping space is heating up; rivals such as OpenAI and Meta have launched agentic AI assistants that can shop online on the user’s behalf.
  • Shopify recently announced it is opening its platform to allow more AI agents to browse and purchase from Shopify listings.
  • Big Tech players are entering this race on the bet that the future of online shopping involves having a robot do most of the work for you.

#Google #AIShopping #UniversalCart #Ecommerce

Source: Google launches its ‘universal’ online shopping cart ahead of the holidays

item.title: Shopify Expands Catalog Access to AI Agents for Automated Shopping and Checkout
item.description:
Shopify Expands Catalog Access to AI Agents for Automated Shopping and Checkout

Shopify announced Tuesday it will allow shoppers to configure AI agents to purchase products on their behalf, giving these agents access to a catalog of over a billion listings. This development marks an expansion of the company’s agentic commerce ambitions, moving beyond a previous exclusive partnership with Meta’s Muse agent. Users can now utilize any AI agent for browsing and purchasing without a specific partnership integration.

🔍 Overview

Shopify is marketing the new feature as a “personal shopper” that can act on a human’s behalf. The agent has access to a catalog consisting of items located both on and off Shopify storefronts. This move follows an earlier partnership announced in September with Meta to allow the Muse agent to browse and purchase items.

🧩 How it works

To enable automated shopping, customers must connect an AI agent to their account on Shop, a Shopify-owned platform designed to consolidate orders and track packages.

  • Integration: The agent connects directly to the user’s Shop account.
  • Checkout: Transactions occur via the one-click Shop Pay feature within the conversation with the agent.
  • Order Management: Any orders placed by the agent are funneled back to the Shop app for tracking.

⚙️ Key details

Humans remain in control of the agent’s behavior through specific rules and required authorizations:

  • Budget Guardrails: Users can set spending limits for the agent.
  • Shipping Preferences: Users can instruct agents to only display products with fast shipping.
  • Purchase Approval: Buyers are required to approve each purchase before it is finalized.

💡 Why it matters

E-commerce has emerged as a significant battleground for AI development, with companies like Google and Amazon also investing in tools where the end goal is an autonomous agent purchasing items for users. This shift has also sparked conflict between major commerce players and AI companies, such as the ongoing dispute between Amazon and firms like Perplexity and Meta over whether agents should be permitted to shop on a customer’s behalf.

#Shopify #AIagents #ECommerce #ShopPay #AgenticCommerce

Source: Shopify opens its catalog up to more AI agents

item.title: Reactiv uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to automate Shopify app updates
item.description:
Reactiv uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to automate Shopify app updates

Reactiv has updated its mobile commerce product by implementing an AI Scheduler to autonomously update merchant apps on a schedule. By utilizing Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Reactiv reduced merchant configuration time by 80 percent and reached production 33 percent faster.

🔍 Overview

Reactiv provides Shopify merchants with native iOS and Android apps, which see shopper conversion rates 2–4 times higher than web visitors. Their toolset includes analytics dashboards, a low-code app builder, and AI-powered features.

🧩 How it works

Reactiv built the AI Scheduler as a three-agent system using the Strands Agents SDK on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The system consists of:

  • Supervisor: Classifies intent.
  • Analytics Agent: Queries merchant data.
  • Builder Agent: Generates configurations.

Reactiv packages its Strands agent graph as a Docker image, pushes it to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), and deploys it to AgentCore. The system later unified interactive and scheduled agents onto a single stack to achieve shared memory across both modes.

⚙️ Key details

Reactiv migrated its configuration schema server (the Config MCP) from Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime. The MCP operates as a stateful server that initializes the current app configuration at the start of a session, with the Builder Agent performing mutations validated against the schema on every call.

Component Function
AgentCore runtime Handles managed agent execution
AgentCore memory Provides persistent cross-session context
AgentCore Identity Handles service-to-service authentication
Amazon EventBridge Provides Cron scheduling
Amazon Bedrock Provides foundation model access and guardrails

Memory and Isolation

AgentCore provides long-term memory scoped per merchant to maintain data privacy, utilizing three specific mechanisms:

  • Session summarizer: Condenses job actions into context for future runs.
  • Preference learner: Tracks merchant approvals or rejections of layouts over time.
  • Semantic fact extractor: Stores knowledge regarding brand guidelines, top sellers, and product categories.

Infrastructure isolation is managed via Firecracker microVMs, ensuring each merchant’s agent state, memory, and execution context runs in its own isolated environment.

#AmazonBedrock #Shopify #AIAgents #Ecommerce #AWS

Source: How Reactiv automates mobile commerce 80% faster with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Amazon Blocks Meta's Muse AI Agent From Shopping on Its Platform
item.description:
Amazon Blocks Meta’s Muse AI Agent From Shopping on Its Platform

Amazon has blocked Meta’s Muse AI agent from shopping on its e-commerce platform on behalf of users. Users began seeing a popup message on Sunday stating that “continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use, to which our customers have agreed.”

⚙️ Key details

Amazon has cited several reasons for the block, including:

  • Lack of Notification: Meta did not notify Amazon that Muse would access its store.
  • Security and Privacy: Amazon expressed concerns over Muse failing to identify itself while browsing and seemingly capturing customer credentials.
  • Operational Transparency: An unnamed Amazon spokesperson told GeekWire, “We think it’s fairly straightforward that third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate."

🔍 Overview

While Meta stated at Muse’s launch earlier this month that the agent cannot see card payment information or secure login details, the agent was previously used during testing to successfully purchase tank tops from Amazon. Additionally, some privacy concerns have emerged since launch, including reports that Muse can see the contents of user messages without the necessary access permission enabled.

💡 Why it matters

This move is part of a broader effort by Amazon to keep customers shopping directly with the retailer and fend off competition from rival agentic AI services. Other related actions include:

  • Legal Action: In November of last year, Amazon sued Perplexity to keep its platform out of the Comet shopping experience, though a judge sided with Perplexity in August.
  • Data Limitation: Since July, Amazon confirmation emails have become sparse, omitting product images and specific item names to limit information being mined by external AI services.

#Meta #Amazon #MuseAI #AIAgents #Ecommerce

Source: Amazon doesn’t trust Meta’s Muse AI agent
